kf1.tip: Rank Nepal's 9,000 deaths, 600,000 buildings destroyed, 3 million homeless and $7 billion loss by long-term harm to the country, defending each place in a line.
kf1.note: There is no single right order. A strong answer weighs how long each harm lasts and what it blocks. Many would put the $7 billion loss first, since a third of GDP leaves less money to rebuild. Three million homeless comes close, as two years later most rural homes were still not rebuilt and camps spread cholera. The trap is ranking deaths first just because they feel worst, without explaining long-term harm to the country.

kf2.tip: Imagine Christchurch kept its fast emergency response and civil defence but had no strict building codes. Say what would follow for the 185 deaths and why.
kf2.note: Most would say deaths would rise sharply. Fast rescue saves people after a collapse, but codes stop the collapse happening. The CTV building alone killed 115 of the 185 because its design flaws let it fall. Without codes, many more buildings could have done the same. A strong answer links this to Nepal, where brick and mud-mortar collapsed. The trap is assuming a quick response could make up for buildings that fail.

cs1.tip: Make the case for and against 'Nepal's 7.8 magnitude, not its brick and mud-mortar buildings, caused its death toll', then decide which side wins.
cs1.note: For magnitude: 7.8 released about 180 times more energy than 6.3, so size played a part. Against: the lesson says size was only part of the reason, and the bigger reason was building quality. Brick and mud-mortar collapsed while reinforced concrete and flexible timber frames did not. Most would decide buildings win, since wealth changes how people meet the geology. The trap is treating it as all one cause or the other.
